archetype: BG -1/-1 counter aristocrats: a converter engine, not a combo deck — Hapatra mints bodies out of other cards' counters, the bodies become cards and drain, and a genuine but narrow combo ceiling sits above a grindy median

candidate_missing_lines.title: The Blowfly family — Blowfly Infestation + Hapatra, + Nest of Scarabs, + Flourishing Defenses
candidate_missing_lines.why_plausible: Three of the bracket_report's 19 two-card infinites, and combo_graph lists Hapatra, Nest of Scarabs and Flourishing Defenses as in-deck Blowfly partners. Oracle chain: Blowfly triggers whenever a creature dies if it had a -1/-1 counter on it, putting a -1/-1 counter on target creature; that placement triggers Hapatra (or Nest, or Defenses) to make a fresh 1/1 token; the 1/1 that received the counter becomes 0/0 and dies with a -1/-1 counter on it, re-triggering Blowfly. This is the deck's headline two-card kill and the one goldfish tracks (16.3% assembled, 12.5% by turn 6) — yet no scenario has ever verified it. A scenario must settle: whether the loop is optional enough to avoid a draw (Blowfly's placement is mandatory but the target is chosen, so the escape is targeting an opponent's creature — 104.4b / 732 territory, exactly the analysis stack 001 step 16 ran for the Druid loop); whether it needs a seed counter and a spare token to start; and what happens when no legal target remains.

candidate_missing_lines.title: Does Mikaeus switch the Blowfly and Hapatra token loops OFF?
candidate_missing_lines.why_plausible: Oracle text, unverified, and it cuts against the deck's own plan. Mikaeus gives other non-Human creatures +1/+1. Snakes, Insects and Elf Warriors are all non-Human, so under Mikaeus they are 2/2 — and a single -1/-1 counter no longer reduces them to 0 toughness. If that reading holds, the token half of every Blowfly loop stops killing its own fodder and the loop terminates, meaning the deck's two flagship engines are mutually exclusive on the battlefield. Stack 001 established that Mikaeus's anthem changes exactly this kind of math for Walking Ballista (step 15, layer 7c), which is why the same question deserves its own resolution for the token loops. This is the highest-value unverified question in the deck.

candidate_missing_lines.title: The Ivy Lane family — Scurry Oak + Ivy Lane Denizen, and the six outlet-paired Ivy Lane entries
candidate_missing_lines.why_plausible: bracket_report names 'Scurry Oak + Ivy Lane Denizen' as the deck's highest-bracket line and stack 001 deliberately declined to rest the bracket floor on it, calling it unverified and noting it comes from the same source whose Mikaeus half failed six times over. The Scurry Oak pairing reads clean on oracle text (Ivy Lane puts a +1/+1 counter on target when another green creature enters; Scurry Oak makes a 1/1 green Squirrel whenever one or more +1/+1 counters are put on it; the Squirrel is a green creature entering) but is a 'may' at the Squirrel step and produces no win without a converter. The other six — Ivy Lane paired with Ashnod's Altar, Phyrexian Altar, Viscera Seer, Carrion Feeder, Blasting Station or Yahenni — look like the same projection artifact that inflated the Mikaeus count: on the named pair alone none of those outlets causes a green creature to ENTER, so Ivy Lane never triggers and no loop exists without Scurry Oak as an unlisted third piece. Verify the Scurry Oak pairing; audit the other six.

candidate_missing_lines.title: Yawgmoth + Hapatra without Mikaeus — the deck's most realistic actual kill
candidate_missing_lines.why_plausible: combo_graph lists Hapatra as an in-deck Yawgmoth partner, and stack 001 verified Yawgmoth's mechanics only inside the Mikaeus line. Oracle chain without Mikaeus: sacrifice a Snake to Yawgmoth, put the -1/-1 counter on a creature that survives it (a big body of yours, or an opponent's creature), Hapatra sees the placement and makes a replacement Snake — net Snake count flat, one card drawn, one life paid, one death trigger per activation. That is a life-and-library-bounded engine that draws your deck and drains the table with any converter out, and it needs neither Mikaeus nor Blowfly. It may well be the line the deck actually wins with most often, and it has never been resolved. The scenario must settle the target-survives requirement, the fizzle rule stack 001 step 12 identified (one instance of 'target', so an illegal target means no draw at all), and the life/library bound.

candidate_missing_lines.title: Hapatra + Host of the Hereafter
candidate_missing_lines.why_plausible: A bracket_report two-card infinite and Host's ONLY combo_graph partner in the entire graph (1 total partner, verified). Oracle chain: a Snake carrying a -1/-1 counter dies, Host moves its counters onto another creature you control, that placement triggers Hapatra to make a fresh Snake, the recipient Snake goes to 0 toughness and dies carrying the counter, Host triggers again. Plausible and elegant, and turns on two things a scenario must decide: whether Host's counter-moving counts as 'putting' counters for Hapatra's trigger, and whether 'up to one target creature you control' gives a clean loop exit.

candidate_missing_lines.title: Necroskitter + Black Sun's Zenith as a one-sided wipe-and-steal
candidate_missing_lines.why_plausible: Not a combo_graph entry — Necroskitter is verified absent from the partners map — so this is pure oracle reasoning and needs verification before being presented as a play. Black Sun's Zenith puts X -1/-1 counters on each creature; opposing creatures that die with a counter on them should each give Necroskitter's optional return trigger, while Hapatra sees one placement per creature. The interaction to resolve is the SBA timing (do the deaths all happen in one check, and does Necroskitter's 'may return that card' see them from the graveyard), plus how many Snake triggers Hapatra actually gets from a single mass placement. If it works, it is the deck's single best card against a creature-based table.

distribution_notes: Read from cards.json, build_plan.json and goldfish_metrics.json. Curve is genuinely low: 64 nonland entries with a mean mana value of 2.19, distributed 4 zero-drops / 16 one / 19 two / 17 three / 6 four / 1 five (Flourishing Defenses) / 1 six (Mikaeus). That hits strategy:deckbuilding.curve's 'build to hit 2, 4 and 6 mana reliably' cleanly — goldfish mean available mana is 2.46 on turn 2, 4.71 on turn 4 and 6.15 on turn 6, so Mikaeus is a real turn-6 card and everything else is castable ahead of schedule. Mana base: 36 lands, zero entering tapped, 29 sources of each colour against a hypergeometric target of 22, 96.2% on-curve for both pips, plus 11 ramp slots including three zero-cost rocks. That is above the Burgess starting point strategy:deckbuilding.mana-base quotes (31 + colours + commander mana value = 35) and it shows: keep-first-seven 79.9%, mean mulligans 0.243, commander cast on turn 2 in 9,970 of 10,000 runs. The cost is concentrated in land quality — roughly a dozen of the 24 distinct lands lead with colourless and only pay colour at a premium, and three are painlands — which is the exact tax strategy:deckbuilding.mana-base names ('a utility land that can't produce the colour you need is not a source'); the hypergeometric check clears it, but it is why land-drop hit rate slides to 64.9% by turn 5 and 54.0% by turn 6 without hurting the plan. Roles: 25 creatures, 8 draw, 8 tutor, 11 ramp, 8 removal, 2 sweepers, 4 protection, 2 recursion, 3 dedicated wincons, 17 flex. Against strategy:deckbuilding.ratios and strategy:deckbuilding.interaction-suite the count is one card under Walser's 15-20 interactive baseline (14) — but the count is not the real departure; the breadth is. Threat density passes on Zupke's floor of at least three finishers (Blood Artist, Zulaport Cutthroat, Bastion of Remembrance, plus Blasting Station and Obelisk Spider as converters) and passes strongly on Eisenherz's layering test from strategy:deckbuilding.threat-density: the combo families are not unconnected, because every one of them terminates in the same drain-converter class and draws on the same sacrifice-outlet and -1/-1-counter pools. The one class that is NOT redundant is the one everything depends on: free repeatable -1/-1 sources number two (Yawgmoth, and Devoted Druid only under Mikaeus). Eight tutors are what make a two-deep class playable at all — a tutor is 'essentially an additional copy of any card in our deck' (strategy:deckbuilding.redundancy-vs-tutors) — and goldfish confirms a tutor is drawn 78.0% of games, 67.6% by turn 6. Finally, the two goldfish targets that matter most tell the whole story of what this deck is: 'commander plus any -1/-1 payoff' assembles 67.2% of the time by mean turn 3.62, while 'Hapatra + Blowfly' assembles 16.3% and 'Mikaeus + a free sacrifice outlet' 9.5% — and that last figure now overstates its own value, since stack 001 refuted six of the eight Mikaeus lines that target was built to track.

engines.engine: The mint, not the source. Her second ability is the passive half that matters — every counter placement anywhere becomes a 1/1 deathtouch Snake, so she is the exchange rate between someone else's -1/-1 counter and a body. Her combat trigger is the weak half and should be treated as a bonus, never a plan. She is also the deck's most reliable card: cast on turn 2 in 9,970 of 10,000 goldfish runs (mean 2.007, 99.9% by turn 6).
engines.evidence: oracle text (two abilities: combat-damage trigger + 'Whenever you put one or more -1/-1 counters on a creature, create a 1/1 green Snake creature token with deathtouch'); verified stack 001 step 11 classifies the first ability as combat-damage-only; goldfish_metrics commander block

engines.engine: The deck's only free repeatable -1/-1 source, and therefore the real tutor target. The verified stack's outlet census — re-derived by the adversarial checker from every 'sacrific' card in cards.json — found eight mana-free sacrifice outlets (Ashnod's Altar, Phyrexian Altar, Carrion Feeder, Viscera Seer, Yahenni, Yawgmoth, Blasting Station, Lazotep Quarry) and exactly one of them also places a -1/-1 counter. With Mikaeus it resets undying via counter annihilation and loops for real, but it is library-bounded by its own mandatory draw: 'a strong engine, not a true infinite'. Each activation costs 1 life, draws a card, and needs a legal target on resolution — the single instance of 'target' means an illegal target fizzles the whole ability, so a second body is mandatory.
engines.evidence: verified stack 001 steps 10 and 12 (checker verdict pass, 4 iterations); oracle text; combo_graph in-deck partners for Yawgmoth: Bastion of Remembrance, Blood Artist, Hapatra, Mikaeus, Nest of Scarabs, Obelisk Spider, Scurry Oak, Sephiroth, Zulaport Cutthroat

engines.engine: The deck's one verified true two-card infinite — of deaths, -1/-1 placements, Snakes and drain, explicitly NOT of mana. Steady state without haste is four counter placements and one death per cycle, zero mana, because the returned Druid is a new object that has not been under your control since your turn began (302.6 blocks its tap ability). First pass yields three green, every pass after yields none. Lightning Greaves or Swiftfoot Boots restore the mana as a three-card, main-phase-only line (nets 4 green with Greaves, 3 with Boots) — but Greaves' shroud then shuts Hapatra and Yawgmoth out of targeting the Druid.
engines.evidence: verified stack 001 steps 13-14, 16 (checker verdict pass; the nine-step haste cycle and the zero-mana steady state were independently re-derived)

engines.engine: The cleanest verified kill in the deck, and a three-card assembly, not two. Mikaeus's +1/+1 is a layer-7c modification applied alongside counters, so a counterless Ballista is a 1/1 under Mikaeus and 704.5f never fires — the classic self-killing pattern is switched off and an external free outlet is mandatory. Per iteration: 1 damage plus whatever the outlet yields. Genuinely unbounded and it converts to a win without needing any drain payoff at all.
engines.piece: Mikaeus, the Unhallowed + Walking Ballista + any free sacrifice outlet

engines.engine: The converter class — the only cards that turn any of the loops into a win, and the axis on which the multiplayer correction bites. Zulaport, Bastion and Obelisk Spider drain EACH opponent; Blood Artist drains one target player per death and is therefore a value card and a wrath-tax, not a table clock. Obelisk Spider is the outlier: it drains on counter PLACEMENT rather than on death, so it converts the Druid loop four times faster than a death-trigger drain does. This is the class 'that should do something to all three seats or win the game'.
engines.evidence: oracle text (all four); verified stack 001 step 16 confirms Blood Artist converts the Druid loop at one life per cycle from a player of your choice; goldfish target 'Any drain converter' 51.9% / 41.5% by turn 6
engines.piece: Zulaport Cutthroat / Bastion of Remembrance / Obelisk Spider (and Blood Artist, one tier down)

engines.engine: The bodies-to-cards layer that carries the median game when no loop exists. Snakes are 1/1, so Skullclamp is a two-card draw for {1} on every one of them; Grim Haruspex draws off every nontoken death; Deadly Dispute and Village Rites turn a Snake into two cards at instant speed. This is what makes the deck an engine rather than a combo pile, and it is the reason a wrath is survivable.
engines.evidence: oracle text; combo_graph in-deck partners for Skullclamp: Ashnod's Altar, Mikaeus, Phyrexian Altar, Pitiless Plunderer; synergy_graph lists Sephiroth as an in-deck Hapatra partner (score 4: Tokens + Sacrifice, -1/-1 + Death Trigger, Flying + Damage Trigger, Attack Trigger + Tokens)
engines.piece: Skullclamp + Grim Haruspex + Morbid Opportunist + Deadly Dispute + Village Rites + Sephiroth

engines.engine: The asymmetric-sweeper package: Black Sun's Zenith puts X -1/-1 counters on EACH creature, which triggers Hapatra once per creature and hands Necroskitter every opposing creature that dies with a counter on it. One card can be a one-sided wipe, a Snake wave and a mass reanimation at once. Sharp caveat verified from oracle text: Toxic Deluge gives -X/-X until end of turn and places no counters, so it triggers neither Hapatra nor Necroskitter nor Nest of Scarabs — it is a pure reset button and should be sequenced as one.
engines.evidence: oracle text (Black Sun's Zenith, Toxic Deluge, Necroskitter, Serrated Arrows, Contagion Clasp); Necroskitter verified ABSENT from combo_graph partners (checked)
engines.piece: Necroskitter + Black Sun's Zenith / Serrated Arrows / Contagion Clasp

engines.engine: The consistency purchase that makes a two-deep enabler class playable: k tutors plus the card act like k+1 copies of every card. Goldfish has a tutor drawn 78.0% of games, 67.6% by turn 6, mean turn 2.70. Post-refutation the correct default target changes — it is not any particular altar but a free repeatable -1/-1 source, and failing that a drain converter. Diabolic Intent and Survival cost you a body/card, which is nearly free in this shell; Green Sun's Zenith fetching Devoted Druid or Ivy Lane Denizen straight to the battlefield is the tempo line.
engines.evidence: build_plan role_budget tutor: 8; goldfish target 'Any tutor drawn' 0.780 / 0.676 by turn 6; verified stack 001 final_state names the free repeatable -1/-1 source as the tutor target that matters; oracle text
engines.piece: The eight-tutor package (Demonic Tutor, Vampiric Tutor, Imperial Seal, Worldly Tutor, Survival of the Fittest, Green Sun's Zenith, Diabolic Intent, Grim Tutor)

gaps: No section on auditing a combo list — the difference between a graph-listed two-card infinite and a line that actually works in YOUR 99 is the single most load-bearing idea in this deck's frame, and the doc has nothing on it. Wanted: how to price an unverified combo count, why pairwise combo data silently drops third pieces and assumes commanders, and what a deck's 'verified kill count' should do to its self-image and its bracket conversation.

No aristocrats / sacrifice-engine section. The outlet / fodder / converter taxonomy, the distinction between free and mana-costed outlets, why a free repeatable outlet is a different card class from a costed one, and the drain-converter tiering (each-opponent versus single-target) all had to be derived here from oracle text. strategy:critical-mass.storm-math is the nearest neighbour and it is about spell velocity, not body velocity.

No counters-matter section. -1/-1 counters as removal that pays you, counter annihilation as a resource, the anthem-versus-shrink anti-synergy (an anthem that makes your own fodder too big to die to your own removal), and the difference between counter-based and stat-modifying mass removal (Black Sun's Zenith versus Toxic Deluge) are all real strategic content with no home in the doc.

No tutor-sequencing section for pilots. strategy:deckbuilding.redundancy-vs-tutors covers the deckbuilding count well but says nothing about the in-game decision: with eight tutors and a two-deep enabler class, WHAT you fetch and WHEN — source before converter, converter before protection, and how a refuted primary target should rewrite the default — is a distinct skill.

No fast-mana section. Mana Vault, Grim Monolith, Chrome Mox, Mox Diamond, Lotus Petal and Dark Ritual each trade a real resource (a card, an untap step, life, a land) for speed, and the doc has no framework for when that trade is correct versus when it is the reason you lose to the first piece of interaction.
Note for the record: the stax gap flagged in the goblin-storm frame is now CLOSED — strategy:threat-assessment.resource-denial covers playing under stax well and was used here.

matchup_frames.vs_aggro: Your best matchup, and mostly for a reason that never shows up in a removal count. A 1/1 deathtouch Snake is virtual interaction: it blanks any attacker regardless of size, so a board of Snakes turns an opposing creature deck's best cards into cards they cannot profitably use (strategy:card-advantage.virtual — 'a card that blanks several opposing cards generates advantage without drawing anything', and in Commander that advantage triples across three seats). Behind that, Black Sun's Zenith and Toxic Deluge are catch-up buttons and Necroskitter converts their aggression into your board. Life is spendable here and this deck spends it constantly — Yawgmoth activations, Phyrexian Reclamation, The One Ring's burden counters, Bitterblossom, Toxic Deluge's additional cost, three painlands — so track which single opponent's clock is real and defend against that one, not the table (strategy:life-as-resource, strategy:multiplayer.pod-management). Do not convert the good matchup into a bad seat by attacking with Hapatra into open blockers for a marginal counter trigger.
matchup_frames.vs_combo: Symmetrically thin and you should play it as a race, not an interaction game. You have no counterspell and no way to touch an artifact or enchantment combo, so the only combo decks you can interact with are creature-based ones — and there you do have instant-speed answers worth holding (Grim Affliction, Fume Spitter's free sacrifice, Walking Ballista's ping, Serrated Arrows). The answer-economy rule inverts here: held answers rot, and against combo the last profitable moment is now (strategy:threat-assessment.answer-economy). Rank combo proximity above every board threat and re-rank every turn (strategy:threat-assessment). Your counter-race is real but not fast: the Blowfly assembly is 16.3% overall and 12.5% by turn 6 (mean turn 4.10) and is itself unverified, so do not plan to out-speed a dedicated combo deck on raw assembly — plan to be the deck the table's interaction is NOT pointed at, deploy Snakes that read as defensive, and take your window while three players are watching each other (strategy:multiplayer.threat-deflection). One caution specific to this list: your 11 Game Changers are the tell. The moment a Mox, a Demonic Tutor or The One Ring hits the table, the deflection budget the Snakes bought you is spent.
matchup_frames.vs_creature_midrange: The default pod seat and the one the deck is actually built for. You out-grind fair creature decks on two axes at once: their removal is bad against tokens, and their attacks are bad into deathtouch. Hold single-target removal until a threat is pointed at you rather than spending it on sight — every one-for-one you cast in a four-player game is a net gift to two bystanders (strategy:multiplayer.asymmetry, strategy:threat-assessment.answer-economy). Win by out-carding them with the Snake-to-cards layer, then pivot the moment a table-wide drain converter joins a repeatable counter source.
matchup_frames.vs_stax: This is where the architect's flagged departure gets its bill. The interactive suite covers exactly one of the five permanent classes: eight removal slots, two sweepers and four protection slots all answer creatures, and a scan of all 88 card entries confirms there is no artifact removal, no enchantment removal, no counterspell and no land answer — the only graveyard-touching effect in the deck is Abstergo Entertainment's {3}, {T}, exile-itself ability. Against Sphere effects, Winter Orb, Blood Moon or a Rest-in-Peace-style hoser you have no answer at all, which is precisely the breadth failure strategy:deckbuilding.interaction-suite warns about: 'Stax is the hardest breadth test... some answers must be castable under the tax.' The honest read is that role assignment is forced — you do not own the long game under an assembling lock, so you are the beatdown racing the lock's completion (strategy:threat-assessment.resource-denial) — and your outs are speed, politics, and someone else's removal. Name them on turn one and sequence to protect them (strategy:resource-hedging.playing-to-outs). Two things genuinely favour you: your kill is cheap and your commander lands turn 2 in 99.7% of goldfish runs, so you can often be under the lock before the second and third pieces layer.
matchup_frames.vs_sweeper_control: You are structurally well-placed and should still sequence carefully. Your board is mostly free tokens; Bitterblossom rebuilds every upkeep for 1 life, Skullclamp and Grim Haruspex convert the loss into cards, and Blood Artist triggers on ANY creature dying, so a table wrath with Blood Artist out is a large drain aimed wherever you like. That is 'buy resilience instead of restraint' already paid for at deckbuild time (strategy:resource-hedging.wrath-math). The asymmetry is in the other direction: your engine pieces — Hapatra, Yawgmoth, Devoted Druid, Ivy Lane Denizen, Scurry Oak, Necroskitter — are all creatures, so a wrath is nearly one-sided against your combo half while being cheap against your token half. So deploy in waves, lead with the token half, and hold the combo half in hand until the pivot window; assume the wrath, because over a four-player game one is near-certain. Your own Black Sun's Zenith is a rebuild, not just a reset — it is the one sweeper that feeds Hapatra, Nest of Scarabs and Necroskitter, while Toxic Deluge feeds none of them.

overall_assessment: This deck is playing a converter's game, and the most useful thing anyone can tell its pilot is that Hapatra is not an engine — she is a mint. She does not generate -1/-1 counters at will (verified stack 001 step 11: that half of her is a combat-damage trigger on an unevasive 2/2); she monetises counters that other cards place, at a rate of one deathtouch body each. That inverts the usual reading of the list. The scarce half is the counter SOURCE, not the outlet, not the payoff — and stack 001's census found exactly one free repeatable source among the deck's eight mana-free sacrifice outlets (Yawgmoth), plus Devoted Druid under Mikaeus. Everything downstream — Snakes, Insects, Elf Warriors, Skullclamp draws, Blood Artist drains, Necroskitter steals — is abundant and redundant. So the tutor target is a source; the mulligan test is 'does this hand contain a route to a repeatable source', not 'does it contain a payoff' (strategy:mulligans.engine-hands: payoffs without the enabler are blanks until the engine exists). The second thing to tell the pilot is that the bracket-4 self-image needs downgrading while the bracket-4 classification does not. The floor of 4 is safe — 11 Game Changers alone carry it, and Brackets 4-5 restrict nothing but the banned list (strategy:deckbuilding.power-level.barometers) — but the '19 two-card infinites' number that supplied a third of the justification is inflated. Four resolver passes and four adversarial checks (checker verdict: pass) refuted six of the eight Mikaeus entries outright: a Snake token ceases to exist before its undying trigger is even placed on the stack, and a non-token creature returned by undying comes back with a +1/+1 counter, which is worth exactly one extra death, not a loop. Two survive — Mikaeus + Devoted Druid as a true infinite of deaths, counters and Snakes but explicitly NOT of mana, and Mikaeus + Walking Ballista as a real but three-card kill — and a third, Yawgmoth, loops for real while being library-bounded by its own mandatory draw. Of the remaining eleven listed lines, the six outlet-paired Ivy Lane entries look like the same projection artifact (none of those outlets makes a green creature enter, so Ivy Lane never triggers without Scurry Oak), and the three Blowfly entries, the Scurry Oak pairing and Hapatra + Host of the Hereafter are simply unresolved. Zero of them may be spoken of as fact. What that leaves is a deck whose ceiling and median are further apart than its build plan believes, which is exactly the discipline strategy:critical-mass.storm-math and strategy:deckbuilding.threat-density both insist on: separate ceiling from median, pace for the median, hold the ceiling as opportunism. The median here is strong — a turn-2 commander in 99.7% of runs, a payoff alongside her 67.2% of the time by mean turn 3.6, and a Snake-to-cards layer deep enough to out-draw three players (strategy:card-advantage) — and the ceiling is a genuine, if narrower, kill. Play it as an engine deck in the control seat that owns inevitability once a table-wide converter is live (strategy:whos-the-beatdown.metagame-clock), keep the perceived threat level under the actual one for as long as the Game Changers let you (strategy:multiplayer.threat-deflection), and take one clean, counted pivot window rather than the first loop that looks like it works (strategy:multiplayer.pivot-window). The build's deliberate departure — 14 interactive slots, all pointed at creatures — is licensed by strategy:critical-mass's 'interaction slots are the price of the engine', and the licence is half-honoured: that section says the linear deck's defence is 'speed, redundancy, and resilience, not answers', and this deck delivers speed and resilience in abundance. It does not deliver breadth, and strategy:deckbuilding.interaction-suite is explicit that breadth comes before depth because 'three opponents mean every permanent type appears'. The correct price to put on the departure is therefore not one card below a template count; it is that the deck has no line whatsoever against permanent-based prison and artifact/enchantment combo, and pays for that with a matchup family it must race or politick rather than answer. That is a legitimate bracket-4 trade against a creature-heavy pod and a losing one against a prison pod — which makes it a Rule 0 conversation, not a build error.

role_assignment.default_role: Control/engine seat by default. You own a medium-to-long game: a repeatable counter source feeding a table-wide drain converter is 'an engine that scales', which strategy:whos-the-beatdown.metagame-clock names as a source of inevitability, and 1/1 deathtouch Snakes make your early turns cheap to survive. Do not try to be the beatdown with combat — Hapatra is a 2/2 with no evasion whose first ability is a combat-damage trigger (verified stack 001 step 11: it is 'not an at-will repeatable placement' and buys at most one extra iteration per combat), and ~120 combined life behind three defences kills incremental damage plans outright (strategy:multiplayer.asymmetry). Role is seat-relative and re-asked per turn cycle (strategy:whos-the-beatdown): against a faster combo or an assembling stax deck you are forced into the racing seat and must tutor for the kill rather than the grind (strategy:threat-assessment.resource-denial).
role_assignment.pivot_trigger: Pivot to all-out win attempt when BOTH halves are live: a free repeatable -1/-1 source (Yawgmoth, or Mikaeus + Devoted Druid) AND a converter that hits every seat (Zulaport Cutthroat, Bastion of Remembrance, Obelisk Spider — Blood Artist drains only one player per death and is a value card, not a table clock). Goldfish sets the honest odds: any drain converter drawn 51.9% overall / 41.5% by turn 6 (mean turn 3.34), while the free-repeatable-source class is two cards deep. Secondary trigger: the Blowfly line assembled (16.3% / 12.5% by turn 6, mean turn 4.10) — that one is not yet verified and is flagged below. Fire when the table's interaction is counted and spent, not when the board looks impressive; at bracket 4 assume every held answer appears the moment you present the loop (strategy:multiplayer.pivot-window). Prefer the attempt that leaves a rebuilt position — Snakes, Bitterblossom and Blood Artist make a failed attempt cheap (strategy:resource-hedging).
